summary: A short cover note from BBN attaching a map of the ARPANET as of the end of December 1972. The ovals show which host computers were thought to connect to each IMP, and sites were asked to report errors or changes. The map itself was a drawing and is not part of the text.

plainLanguage.summary: A map of the early network showing which computers plugged into which gateway boxes, with a request to tell the mapmaker if anything was wrong.

subtitle: A snapshot of the ARPANET's physical connections in late 1972.

tldr.problem: Early ARPANET researchers needed to know which computers were physically connected to which network interface machines (IMPs) at each site.
tldr.mechanism: BBN published a logical map showing the network topology as of December 1972, with ovals representing host computers connected to each IMP, and requested that sites report any errors or planned changes.
tldr.outcome: The map served as a reference for understanding the ARPANET's structure at that time and coordinating further growth.

today: This RFC is a historical document from the ARPANET era. The map it references was not preserved in machine-readable form, but the RFC serves as documentation of the network's topology at that moment.

sections.title: The ARPANET Map
sections.content: RFC 432 is a short cover note from Bolt Beranek and Newman (BBN), the organization managing the early ARPANET, announcing a logical map of the network as of December 30, 1972. The ovals in the map indicate the host computers connected to each IMP (Interface Message Processor, the network's routing devices). Double ovals represent connections through an interface.
sections.plainLanguage: A short letter introducing a drawing of the network, showing which computers were connected where.

sections.title: Purpose and Coordination
sections.content:
The RFC requests that recipients review the map for accuracy and notify BBN of any errors in the network topology or planned changes to their site's connections in the coming months. Contact information is provided for Nancy Neigus at BBN's Cambridge office, including a telephone extension and instructions to leave messages at the NIC (Network Information Center).

This coordination mechanism was essential for the early ARPANET, where changes to the physical network required careful tracking and notification across all participating sites.
sections.plainLanguage: BBN asked everyone to check the map and call if something was wrong or if they were adding more computers.

sections.title: A Moment in ARPANET History
sections.content: This RFC captures the ARPANET's state in the early 1970s, when the network was still relatively small and the complete topology could fit on a single map. As the network grew, such centralized maps became impractical and more sophisticated network management and discovery mechanisms developed.
sections.plainLanguage: This map shows the network when it was still small enough to draw on one page.
